data.feature_description_html:
Microsoft Copilot Integrated into Power BI and Microsoft FabricCopilot experiences have emerged across the applications people use every day, bringing AI closer to the work happening in each product. But this can also feel fragmented, with different entry points, separate conversations, and uncertainty about which Copilot agent to use.

Our goal is to create a consistent Copilot experience that is available wherever people work. No one should have to leave the application they are using to find it. Microsoft Copilot should come into their experience, carry context with them, and connect to the specialized intelligence of each product. This release will allow tenant admins the opportunity to choose Microsoft Copilot as an alternative to the Power BI standalone Copilot experience, bringing all of M365 into Power BI for licensed users.

One Familiar Place for Context and Trusted Data

This integration gives users one familiar place to bring together business context and trusted data. Shared conversation history lets them continue a discussion as they move between Microsoft Copilot experiences instead of starting over in each application.

For someone starting in Power BI, a question no longer has to stop with the numbers in a report. A sales leader could use Fabric IQ to identify which regions are behind plan, then use Work IQ to connect the results with customer emails, meetings, account plans, and documents.

They could summarize the complete picture and even kick off actions and tasks in Cowork, all from inside Power BI. This work context and ability to move directly from insight to action were not available in the standalone Power BI Copilot experience.

Administrator Controls

A new setting in the Fabric admin portal will determine whether this integration is available by enabling or disabling the entry point in the navigation pane.

The setting will be off by default, giving administrators time to evaluate the experience before introducing it to their organization. Administrators can enable it when they are ready and disable it if they need to pause access.

This setting is independent of the existing setting for standalone Power BI Copilot:

  • If both settings are enabled, users with a Microsoft 365 Copilot license will see entry points for both experiences. Standalone Power BI Copilot will continue to appear on Home.
  • If standalone Power BI Copilot is disabled and Microsoft 365 Copilot is enabled, users will see only the Microsoft 365 Copilot entry point.

Initial Public Preview Availability

During the initial public preview, the integrated experience is available only to users with a Microsoft 365 Copilot license.

These users receive the full Copilot Chat experience in Power BI and Fabric, bringing together:

  • Fabric data through Fabric IQ
  • Relevant Microsoft 365 context through Work IQ

Existing permissions and governance controls continue to determine which content each user can access.

data.blog_title: Introducing capacity overage: Flexibility when you need it most (Preview)
data.feature_description: Fabric capacity overage is an opt-in feature in Microsoft Fabric that automatically bills for excess capacity usage in a pay-as-you-go basis instead of throttling operations - enabling capacity administrators to protect capacities from being throttled.  Today, as a capcity admin, you can use surge protection, resize capacities, or pay for dedicated capacities to try to protect mission critical jobs, but all these approaches still can result in throttling and rejection due to insufficient provisioned capacity.  Overage billing addresses this consideration.  The solution allows a capacity admin to opt-in to paying off their smoothed usage and overages instead of being throttled.As Microsoft releases Fabric Overage Billing the Capacity Metrics App will be updated to reflect this new capability.  Specifically, views this will include clear visibility into overage events, showing when Overage Billing was activated and overage charges are being assessed - as well as cases where the capacity is reaching the overage billing limits set and is experiencing throttling.  The view also will show trends over time alongside the amount of utilization.  These enhancements, alongside the core Overage Billing capability, make it easier to monitor costs, optimize resource allocation, and ensure business continuity through flexible capacity management capabilities.  There will also be a new ARM API for Capacity Creation that supports Capacity Overage.  There will also be an ability, both as opt-in emails and in-product, to receive notifications when overage activity occurs or subsides.

data.feature_description: # Generally Available: Vector Search and Vector Indexes in Azure SQL Vector Search and Vector Indexes are now generally available in Azure SQL Database. Using the [CREATE VECTOR INDEX](https://learn.microsoft.com/sql/t-sql/statements/create-vector-index-transact-sql?view=sql-server-ver17) and [VECTOR_SEARCH](https://learn.microsoft.com/sql/t-sql/functions/vector-search-transact-sql?view=sql-server-ver17) T-SQL capabilities, you can perform efficient approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) searches for AI scenarios such as semantic search, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), recommendation systems, and image search. data.blog_title: Wondering how to incrementally amass data in your data destination? This is how!
data.feature_description: Customers will be able to configure a backup to store a snapshot of a query's results after every dataflow run, in any of the supported data destinations. Each run writes a new, timestamped file or table into the destination the customer chose, so snapshots accumulate side by side instead of overwriting one another.This gives customers a durable record of what their data looked like at each point in time, which today they can only approximate by building a second dataflow, adding a downstream pipeline, or exporting results by hand. With backups in place, customers can look back at a previous run to understand when and where their data changed, compare a surprising result against the last known good snapshot before escalating it, and satisfy audit or record-keeping requirements that call for evidence of what was produced and when. Because snapshots land in a destination the customer already owns, they can be queried alongside the rest of their data, connected to downstream reports, or shared with colleagues who don't have access to the dataflow itself. Each snapshot is a byproduct of a run the customer is already performing, so the history builds itself with no extra artifacts to maintain and no manual steps to remember.
